sources.title: Dummies
sources.publisher: Better Health Channel, Victorian Department of Health
sources.quote: Give your child the chance to stop their dummy habit when they are ready. Most children stop sucking habits between the ages of two and four, but you can start the process from around one year of age. ... Avoid trying to stop dummy use suddenly, as it can lead to other oral habits such as thumb or finger sucking. ... Limit the use of the dummy to sleep or nighttime. ... Talk about stopping the dummy for a couple of days to prepare your child. ... Consider replacing it with a toy, maybe a cuddly toy they have chosen and can hold when they would be using the dummy. You can talk about the replacement when they are asking for the dummy. ... Persist gently but firmly. The first few days without a dummy are likely to be the most difficult.
sources.supports: Stopping gradually, limiting the dummy to sleep, preparing the child by talking for a couple of days, a chosen cuddly toy in its place and that the first few days are the hardest. An Australian state health service page, applied to Israeli families as general child health advice.

sources.title: Weaning off dummies and bottles
sources.publisher: Sheffield Children's NHS Foundation Trust, Resource Library
sources.quote: Start by just letting your child use their dummy for nap times and bed time. Try to swap it out for their favourite toy or teddy to hold onto for comfort instead. ... Once they are using their dummy less, set a date for being ‘dummy free’. Help them by giving them lots of praise, and give them lots of positive attention. ... Make sure you and other caregivers remove any bottles and dummies from your child’s sight. ... Try creating some fun around leaving the dummy behind. For example use a ‘Dummy Fairy’ that takes it away during the night and leaves a small reward. Remember that this can be a difficult and challenging time for them.
sources.supports: Dummy only for naps and bedtime first, a favourite toy for comfort, a dummy free date once use is down, praise, keeping it out of sight and making the goodbye fun (a Dummy Fairy). An NHS trust leaflet for UK families, used as general advice.

אז בבקשה, לא בבת אחת.
הנה חמישה דברים שיעזרו לי.

תספרו לי כמה ימים לפני.
שאני אדע מה עומד לקרות,
ושיהיה לי זמן להתרגל לרעיון.
מה יעזור לי לשמוע:
״רוני, עוד שלושה לילות נגיד לו ביי.״

ביום הוא נשאר בארון.
בבוקר אני משחקת, הולכת לגן, רצה בחצר,
ולא צריכה אותו בפה כל הזמן.
כשהוא לא מול העיניים, אני שוכחת ממנו.
ובלילה, במיטה, הוא עוד שלי.

הארנב שבחרתי בעצמי.
מה אתם רואים:
אני מבקשת מוצץ, ומתחילה לבכות.
מה קורה לי בפנים:
הידיים שלי מחפשות משהו להחזיק.
אז תזכירו לי את הארנב,
בדיוק אז, כשאני מבקשת.

פיה לוקחת, ומשאירה הפתעה.
שמים אותו ליד המיטה.
אני נרדמת.
בבוקר הוא איננו.
ובמקומו מחכה משהו קטן.
ותגידו לי ״רוני, הצלחת!״

ומה אם אתעורר בלי מוצץ?
הלילות הראשונים הכי קשים לי.
אני אבכה, ואולי אבקש אותו שוב.
מה יעזור לי:
שתהיו רגועים, ותחזיקו מעמד איתי.
בעדינות, אבל בלי להחזיר אותו.

אני עושה צעד גדול.
בשבילכם זה מוצץ קטן.
בשבילי זה הדבר הכי רך בלילה.
אז לאט, עם הרבה חיבוקים,
ועם הארנב ביד,
אני מגיעה לשם בקצב שלי.

אפשר גם לעזור להם
עם הגמילה מהמוצץ
בעזרת ספר מותאם אישית.
תכתבו "מוצץ"

sources.title: Dummies
sources.publisher: Better Health Channel, Victorian Department of Health
sources.quote: Give your child the chance to stop their dummy habit when they are ready. Most children stop sucking habits between the ages of two and four, but you can start the process from around one year of age. ... Avoid trying to stop dummy use suddenly, as it can lead to other oral habits such as thumb or finger sucking. ... Limit the use of the dummy to sleep or nighttime. ... Talk about stopping the dummy for a couple of days to prepare your child. ... Consider replacing it with a toy, maybe a cuddly toy they have chosen and can hold when they would be using the dummy. You can talk about the replacement when they are asking for the dummy. ... Persist gently but firmly. The first few days without a dummy are likely to be the most difficult.
sources.supports: Stopping gradually, limiting the dummy to sleep, preparing the child by talking for a couple of days, a chosen cuddly toy in its place and that the first few days are the hardest. An Australian state health service page, applied to Israeli families as general child health advice.

sources.title: Weaning off dummies and bottles
sources.publisher: Sheffield Children's NHS Foundation Trust, Resource Library
sources.quote: Start by just letting your child use their dummy for nap times and bed time. Try to swap it out for their favourite toy or teddy to hold onto for comfort instead. ... Once they are using their dummy less, set a date for being ‘dummy free’. Help them by giving them lots of praise, and give them lots of positive attention. ... Make sure you and other caregivers remove any bottles and dummies from your child’s sight. ... Try creating some fun around leaving the dummy behind. For example use a ‘Dummy Fairy’ that takes it away during the night and leaves a small reward. Remember that this can be a difficult and challenging time for them.
sources.supports: Dummy only for naps and bedtime first, a favourite toy for comfort, a dummy free date once use is down, praise, keeping it out of sight and making the goodbye fun (a Dummy Fairy). An NHS trust leaflet for UK families, used as general advice.

sources.title: Dummies
sources.publisher: Better Health Channel, Victorian Department of Health
sources.quote: Give your child the chance to stop their dummy habit when they are ready. Most children stop sucking habits between the ages of two and four, but you can start the process from around one year of age. ... Avoid trying to stop dummy use suddenly, as it can lead to other oral habits such as thumb or finger sucking. ... Limit the use of the dummy to sleep or nighttime. ... Talk about stopping the dummy for a couple of days to prepare your child. ... Consider replacing it with a toy, maybe a cuddly toy they have chosen and can hold when they would be using the dummy. You can talk about the replacement when they are asking for the dummy. ... Persist gently but firmly. The first few days without a dummy are likely to be the most difficult.
sources.supports: Stopping gradually, limiting the dummy to sleep, preparing the child by talking for a couple of days, a chosen cuddly toy in its place and that the first few days are the hardest. An Australian state health service page, applied to Israeli families as general child health advice.

sources.title: Weaning off dummies and bottles
sources.publisher: Sheffield Children's NHS Foundation Trust, Resource Library
sources.quote: Start by just letting your child use their dummy for nap times and bed time. Try to swap it out for their favourite toy or teddy to hold onto for comfort instead. ... Once they are using their dummy less, set a date for being ‘dummy free’. Help them by giving them lots of praise, and give them lots of positive attention. ... Make sure you and other caregivers remove any bottles and dummies from your child’s sight. ... Try creating some fun around leaving the dummy behind. For example use a ‘Dummy Fairy’ that takes it away during the night and leaves a small reward. Remember that this can be a difficult and challenging time for them.
sources.supports: Dummy only for naps and bedtime first, a favourite toy for comfort, a dummy free date once use is down, praise, keeping it out of sight and making the goodbye fun (a Dummy Fairy). An NHS trust leaflet for UK families, used as general advice.

post_text.fb_text:
היום יום ההולדת שלי! 🎈
אני קופצת למיטה שלכם עוד בחושך.
בראש שלי כבר יש תמונה:
כל החברים באים ביחד, בדיוק בארבע,
ואני פותחת להם את הדלת.

אתם מספרים לי מה יהיה.
מי יבוא, איפה נשב, מה נעשה קודם.
מה יעזור לי:
גם להגיד לי שחברים מגיעים לאט,
אחד אחד, ולא כולם ביחד.
ושזה בסדר אם משהו משתנה.

אנחנו משחקים ״מסיבה״
אמא משחקת אורחת, ואני פותחת לה.
״שלום, תודה שבאת!״
ומה אם עוד אף אחד לא בא?
אז מחכים, ומציירים ביחד.

הכל מוכן.
הבלונים תלויים, הכוסות על השולחן.
אני בשמלה הוורודה, ליד הדלת.
מחכה לצלצול הראשון.
עוד רגע, עוד רגע.

אף אחד עוד לא בא.
עשרים דקות, וכלום.
הבטן שלי מתכווצת, הדמעות באות,
ואני צועקת ״אף אחד לא אוהב אותי!״
בתמונה שבראש שלי זה לא היה ככה.

פינה שקטה, רק לרגע.
אתם לא אומרים ״זה כלום״.
אתם אומרים ״אנחנו שומעים אותך.״
מה יעזור לי:
פינה שקטה עם שמיכה,
ואחד מכם לידי.

דינג דונג!
החברה שלי מהגן הגיעה, ועוד שניים.
אני מנגבת את העיניים ורצה לפתוח,
בדיוק כמו שהתאמנו בבוקר.
״שלום, תודה שבאת!״

״מה היה הכי כיף?״
אתם שואלים, ואני נזכרת בעוגה,
ובריקודים עם החברה מהגן.
מה יעזור לי לשמוע:
״מיכל, ראינו איך חזרת למסיבה.״

זה לא היה יום מושלם.
אמא ואבא, היו בו דמעות,
והיה בו רגע שחשבתי שאף אחד לא יבוא.
אבל ידעתי מה יכול לקרות,
וידעתי לאן ללכת כשקשה.

אפשר גם לעזור להם
עם האכזבה ביום ההולדת
בעזרת ספר מותאם אישית.
תכתבו "עוגה"
ואשלח לכם קישור להכנת הספר 📖

sources.title: How to Help Your Kids Handle Disappointment
sources.publisher: Child Mind Institute (last reviewed 6 Nov 2023)
sources.quote: Instead, emphasize that you hear your child and express your support for how they're handling this. ... It's also important to avoid judging their reactions. ... invalidating the pain that our children are feeling (by telling them it's not a big deal, for example) ... Working with your child to plan out their days is one way to give them a sense of control over what's happening. ... Let them know that even though this situation is different, they can use some of the same skills to get through it.
sources.supports: Hear and support the child's feeling instead of dismissing it, do not judge the reaction, plan the day together for a sense of control, and point out the skills the child already has. A general page about disappointment, applied to a birthday that does not go to plan.

sources.title: Helping Kids With Flexible Thinking
sources.publisher: Child Mind Institute (Rae Jacobson, last reviewed 8 Mar 2024)
sources.quote: When kids are able to think flexibly about a problem they're less likely to fall apart if things don't go according to plan. ... Let's come up with some awesome ideas for what else we can do if that happens. ... invite them to help you come up with ideas for how to manage uncertainty as well as difficult changes. ... When your child sees you navigate changes or surprises in a reasonable, solution-focused way,
sources.supports: Thinking through what else to do if plans change, asking the child for ideas, and showing a calm solution focused reaction to surprises. A general page, applied to birthdays.

sources.title: How to Take the Stress Out of Family Gatherings
sources.publisher: Child Mind Institute (Rachel Ehmke, last reviewed 7 Oct 2026)
sources.quote: Always have a conversation before leaving your house about how you expect your children to behave ... if things get too overwhelming and intense, there’s a place to take a break and just be quiet. ... Know that no holiday is going to be perfect.
sources.supports: Talk before the event about what is expected, a quiet place to take a break, and that no gathering is perfect. A page about family gatherings, applied to a birthday party by analogy.
